speaker: John Quinn
title: Ep 110 | John B. Quinn | Big Law Litigation Trailblazer & Pioneer
question: How has competition among corporate law firms structurally changed over the past few decades?
guest: I think it's more transparent and more businesslike. The competition is better in the sense that law firms aren't hiding behind just histories and some hocus pocus or mystery. Lawyers have to be able to attract engagements based on their experience and their results—there's more of that than there used to be. I remember attending a bar association dinner in Downtown LA back in the early 1980s with distinguished lawyers on stage, and a senior partner at a major firm launched into a screed about lawyers willing to prostitute themselves to advertise and promote their personal capabilities, holding his nose as he said it. That's nonsense, but that was what it was like then. Now it's not a question of prostituting yourself—it's providing information and arming clients with the information they need to make intelligent decisions about professional relationships and engagements.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Over the past few decades, corporate law has shifted from a relationship-based guild into a competitive, national and increasingly global market for both clients and talent.

Historically, large companies kept long-term ties with one or two firms, partners stayed for life, and pay followed seniority ("lockstep"). Several changes eroded that model. In-house legal departments grew in size and sophistication, with general counsel splitting work among firms, running panels and competitive pitches, and pressing for discounts and alternative fees. Published financial data, starting with the American Lawyer's profits-per-partner rankings in the mid-1980s, made firms comparable and fuelled a lateral market in which rainmaking partners move for higher pay, pushing firms toward "eat what you kill" compensation, non-equity tiers and star-level packages.

Firms responded by scaling through mergers and international expansion, producing a stratified market: a small elite capturing premium transactional and litigation work at very high profitability, and a squeezed middle competing on price. Meanwhile, new rivals emerged, including the Big Four accounting firms, alternative legal service providers, legal technology, and, in some jurisdictions such as England and Australia, outside-owned firms.

points.why: The response describes the erosion of longstanding client relationships but does not establish that firms can no longer win clients on institutional pedigree alone.
The response mentions competitive pitches and financial rankings without tying hiring decisions to lawyers’ proven case outcomes or track records.
The response links financial transparency to lateral hiring among firms without explaining how open promotion of legal capabilities helps clients choose counsel.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Over the past few decades, corporate law has evolved from a sheltered, relationship-driven guild into a fiercely stratified market. Historically, elite firms relied on enduring institutional client ties, unchallenged hourly billing, and lockstep partner pay that discouraged defections. That stability unraveled as corporate legal departments expanded and professionalized, shifting bargaining power to general counsel who unbundled matters, ran competitive pitches, trimmed outside-counsel panels, and moved routine work in-house.

Simultaneously, public profit rankings broke the taboo against poaching, sparking an open lateral market for star rainmakers. To recruit and retain top producers, firms largely abandoned pure lockstep models in favor of performance-based pay and multi-tiered partnerships. Competition has also polarized the profession: global mega-firms and elite private-equity powerhouses now capture the most lucrative, high-stakes transactions and disputes, squeezing traditional midsize practices into mergers or collapse. Meanwhile, alternative legal service providers and legal technology—now accelerated by artificial intelligence—have commoditized routine diligence and contract work, forcing firms to compete on specialized expertise, speed, and efficiency rather than institutional pedigree alone.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Over roughly forty years, competition among corporate law firms has changed from stable, relationship-based arrangements to an open, market-driven contest. In the mid-20th century, large companies usually kept one "outside general counsel" firm for decades. Partners rarely moved between firms, and compensation was often paid in lockstep by seniority. As in-house legal departments grew, companies began buying legal work matter by matter. They hired specialists for each deal or case, cut down their panels of outside firms, and pushed for discounts and alternative fee arrangements.

Starting in 1985, The American Lawyer's rankings made firm revenue and profits per partner public. That fueled a strong lateral market in which partners with large books of business move between firms. Firms responded by weakening lockstep pay, adding non-equity partner tiers and steepening internal pay gaps. The market has split into tiers: a small elite earns premium fees for high-stakes work, while routine work faces price pressure. Mergers, global expansion, salary wars for associates and competition from alternative providers, Big Four accounting firms and legal technology (now including AI) have intensified this. Recently, private-equity-backed structures have added further pressure.

Hiring specialists for individual matters does not establish that clients award engagements based on demonstrated past results.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Over the past few decades, competition among corporate law firms has shifted from a clubby, relationship-driven profession into a transparent, fiercely commercial market. Historically, large corporations relied on a single primary law firm for decades, while firms grew organically through lockstep compensation and lifelong partner loyalty. As companies expanded sophisticated in-house legal departments, general counsel began unbundling work, hiring different firms on a matter-by-matter basis and demanding greater cost accountability. Simultaneously, the rise of public financial rankings like the Am Law 100 made profits per equity partner a central benchmark, fueling an aggressive lateral market in which firms routinely poach rainmaking partners and tie pay to individual origination. The market has also bifurcated: global megafirms compete on scale and cross-border reach, while elite boutiques capture specialized, high-stakes work, squeezing traditional mid-sized firms. Finally, alternative legal service providers, the Big Four, and legal AI have commoditized routine work, forcing firms to compete on efficiency, technology, and specialized expertise rather than institutional inertia.

The response identifies specialized expertise as a competitive factor without tying hiring decisions to demonstrated results or a concrete track record.
The response calls the market transparent without explaining how openly promoting legal capabilities helps clients evaluate and hire counsel.

Competition among corporate law firms has shifted from a largely local, relationship-driven market to a national and increasingly global one. Large firms have expanded through mergers, new offices, and lateral hiring. Partners with portable books of business are more mobile, so firms compete for revenue-generating lawyers as well as for clients. [Galanter and Henderson](https://www.stanfordlawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2010/04/GalanterHenderson.pdf) · [Chambers](https://chambers.com/thought-leadership/law-firm-mergers-consolidation-usa)

Corporate legal departments also have more control over who gets each assignment. Companies increasingly divide work among firms, keep some matters in-house, and send standardized tasks to alternative legal service providers. That has sharpened competition along two lines. Firms handling high-stakes deals and disputes can command premiums for scarce expertise, while providers handling more routine work face greater pressure on price, efficiency, and predictability. noweb.answer:
Corporate law has shifted from a largely local, relationship-driven business to a more global and segmented market. Companies once sent most of their outside legal work to a small circle of firms. Today, larger in-house legal departments compare rates, negotiate fees, and assign matters to different providers based on cost and expertise.

At the top of the market, mergers and international expansion have created firms that compete for cross-border deals and high-stakes disputes. Specialist boutiques compete for some of that same work, while regional firms and alternative legal service providers compete for more standardized assignments. Competition for lawyers has intensified too. Partners with portable client relationships move between firms more readily, so firms compete for revenue by recruiting entire teams as well as by pitching clients directly.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Corporate law firms once competed largely to become a company’s trusted outside counsel. Winning that relationship often meant handling much of its legal work for years. As companies built larger in-house legal departments, they gained the expertise to divide work among firms and choose counsel for each deal, dispute, or specialty. Even a longtime adviser now often has to compete for the next assignment.

Competition for talent has changed, too. Partners with strong client ties can take business with them when they move, so firms increasingly compete by recruiting established partners and entire practice groups. At the same time, the largest firms have expanded across borders to handle complex matters, while specialist firms can compete for a particular assignment without having to serve all of a company’s legal needs.
